---
title: "Learning route and outcomes"
---

## What you should learn

1. Read molecular representations and identify functional groups and charges.
2. Explain properties and reactivity using polarity, resonance and acid–base reasoning.
3. Distinguish conformations and configurations and interpret simple stereochemistry.
4. Draw valid elementary mechanisms that conserve atoms and charge.
5. Predict selected substitution, elimination, addition, redox and carbonyl reactions.
6. Propose a short synthesis and justify conditions and experimental checks.
7. Use simple IR and one-dimensional NMR evidence to distinguish structures.
8. Record, calculate and communicate laboratory results in a reproducible report.

The course syllabus on Canvas gives the formal outcomes and examination rules.

## Week by week

| Week | Topics | What you'll produce |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Structures; properties and IR; acids and bases | Annotated structures, a property explanation, a proton-transfer mechanism and an ionisation plot |
| 2 | Conformations; stereochemistry; mechanisms | Newman and chair drawings, stereochemical comparisons and electron-flow diagrams |
| 3 | Substitution; elimination and addition; alcohols and redox | Reaction predictions, competing pathways and checked reactant amounts |
| 4 | Carbonyl addition; acyl chemistry; amines and aromatics | Stepwise mechanisms, ester/amide comparisons and a TLC evidence table |
| 5 | Spectroscopy; synthesis and evidence; integration | Structure puzzles, a short synthetic route and a report linking claims to evidence |

## How to study a day

Watch the lecture and pause to draw and predict when a "Try it" box appears.
Then do the exercises before opening the hints and worked answers, try the
interactive demo, and finish with the self-check. When you get something
wrong, redraw it correctly and say what changed. Recognising an answer is a
start; being able to construct it yourself is the goal.

The [reading guide](reference/reading.qmd) lists the matching book chapters.

## What comes next?

The course is a foundation for biochemistry. Organic Chemistry II is a
possible follow-on elective for deeper synthesis and reactivity.
